newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Central Bank worried by T-bill yield rise.
newsitem.headline: Russian Central Bank worried by T-bill yield rise.

text.p: The Russian Central Bank is worried by a recent rising trend in yields on the government securities market, bank First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko said on Friday.
"There are some worries about the sharp rise in rates from a certain unusual situation on the government securities market," Aleksashenko told Reuters Financial Television.
Aleksashenko said the instability in yields, which has seen rates rise to the mid-30s on Friday from the upper 20s two weeks ago, had stopped the bank from lowering the refinancing rate.
"The short-term volatility so far has not allowed the Board of Directors to take any decision regarding refinancing rates," he said.
The Central Bank does not actually use the refinancing rate, currently 42 percent, as the basis for a lending facility to commercial banks, but it is seen as a key financial indicator.
Aleksashenko said the bank thought the government was ready to take measures to improve Russia's financial situation though he said low tax collection appeared to be a continuing problem.

"The Central Bank explanation is that the intense indebtedness to the Ministry of Finance raises the needs of the federal budget for funds and, it seems, shows that the situation with taxes, unfortunately, is not improving," he said.
But he said the Central Bank was satisfied with Russia's inflationary trend and expected year-on-year inflation through December to meet targets of 10-12 percent.
Year-on-year inflation slowed to 18.1 percent in February and was 131 percent in December 1995.

Aleksashenko added that macroeconomic stabilisation had prompted the board to lower rouble reserve requirements for commercial banks from May 1. Requirements for funds deposited for up to 30 days would drop to 14 percent from 16 percent.
The rate would lower to 11 percent from 13 percent for funds deposited from 31 to 90 days and for greater than 91 days to eight percent from 10 percent.

Hard currency reserve requirements will rise to six percent from five percent, he said, adding that the bank was following a policy of eliminating the difference between reserve requirements for rouble and hard currency loans.
